amendments.rule: An inflected verb may align to an English subject pronoun, auxiliary, and main verb together. Choose the lexical English verb as the target head. **This permission is specific to a pronoun realizing the verb's person and number.** A lexical English subject noun the ASV supplies where no source nominal is present answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit: `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* gives *shall dwell* to the verb and leaves *men* `added`. **A volitive English frame belongs to the verb whose mood it renders.** Where the ASV expands an imperative or jussive with *Oh* or *Oh that ... would*, the framing words join the verb's unit and the unit heads on its lexical predicate: `הוֹדוּ` → *Oh give thanks* heads on *thanks* under rule 44, and `יוֹדוּ` → *Oh that ... would praise* heads on *praise*. **And the frame need not open with *Oh*.** Where the ASV writes the fixed English acclamation *Long live* for a jussive of `חָיָה`, the *Long* is what English spends on that jussive's optative force and joins the verb's unit on the same terms, headed on *live*: `יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ` → ***Long live*** *the king*. An ASV italic on the *Long* corroborates the supply and decides nothing, by rule 7; the corpus reads `יְחִי` → *Long live* in four units across four chapters, always headed on *live*, and marks the *Long* `added` in none. A lexical subject noun supplied inside such a frame is still `added` under the preceding sentence — *Oh that men would praise* leaves *men* outside the verb's discontinuous unit. This applies only where no optative particle or multi-source optative idiom stands in the Hebrew; a present `לוּ` or `מִי יִתֵּן` takes its own fixed English formula under rule 30. **A presentative dummy *there* is not such a lexical subject.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb or participle with a presentative frame — `יֵּצֵא` → *there came forth*, `נִשֵּׂאת` → *there was lifted up* — the dummy belongs to the verb's unit, by the same constructional reasoning that puts it on `הָיָה` under rule 21, and the unit still heads on the lexical verb. When the verse also has an explicit subject noun, that noun's tokens are its own unit and only a genuinely pleonastic pronoun stays with the verb. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus an explicit subject pronoun as a relative clause, the English *who* or *which* realizes the pronoun; the waw is `unrepresented` if the ASV writes no separate connective.** Do not give the relative pronoun to the waw merely because it opens the recast clause: `וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו` → *which was behind him* gives *which* to `הוּא` and leaves the waw unrepresented, and `וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי` → *who am old* gives *who* to `אֲנִי` on the same terms. **But read whether the relative is what realizes that pronoun before applying that sentence.** What it governs is a recasting in which the pronoun itself becomes the relative, which is why the ASV writes no other word for it and the relative's referent is the pronoun's own. Where instead the ASV writes the pronoun's own English word beside the relative, and the relative points at something else the clause speaks of, the pronoun is holding a rendering of its own and is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, while a relative pointing at another antecedent realizes nothing of it and would head on a word that does not write its lexeme, against rule 24: the pronoun takes the word written for it, the finite verb keeps its auxiliaries and lexical verb, and the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective, exactly as it is where no pronoun stands at all. `וְאַתְּ אָלִית` → *about* ***which*** ***thou*** *didst utter a curse* gives *thou* to `אַתְּ`, *which* to the waw and *didst utter a curse* to the verb, while the supplied *about*, whose relation no morpheme carries, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, since no bare nominal stands for rule 33 to place it on. Read whom the relative refers to and count the clause's English words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; one verse may write both shapes, and JDG.17.2 does, aligning `אֲנִי לָקַחְתִּי` → *I took* with the pronoun holding its own *I*. **A question auxiliary the ASV fronts belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb.** English marks a yes-or-no question by fronting an auxiliary, and where `הֲ` stands in the clause that word is what the ASV has written for it: `הֲלוֹא לֶאֱמוּנָה` → *do not thine eyes look upon truth* gives *do* to `הֲ` in a clause that has no verb at all to take it, and `הַעַל אֵלֶּה לֹא אֶפְקֹד` → *Shall I not visit* gives *Shall* to `הֲ` and *I visit* to the verb, even though that auxiliary also carries the imperfect's future. The `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question is read the same way, since it is what marks that clause as the second question: `אִם לֹא תָחִילוּ` → *will ye not tremble* gives *will* to `אִם` and *ye tremble* to the verb. **But a particle for which the ASV has written a connective of its own is not a home for the auxiliary as well.** Where the ASV renders that `אִם`, or another particle standing at the head of the second question, by a written *Or*, *Or if* or another connective, that word is the particle's under rule 14, the particle takes no second English word, and the fronted auxiliary is the ordinary one this rule's first sentence gives the verb: `אִם יְדַבֵּר אֵלֶיךָ רַכּוֹת` → ***Or*** *will he speak soft words unto thee* gives *Or* to `אִם` and *will he speak* to the verb. This is the reasoning of this rule's second limit below, where an interrogative holding an English word of its own leaves the auxiliary to the verb, and of rule 51's ruling that a waw holding a connective of its own is not a home for a second word. Count the clause's English function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; where the ASV writes no connective for the particle, the preceding sentence governs as before. Where the ASV marks the question by inversion alone and writes no auxiliary, the particle is `unrepresented`: `הַאוֹתִי לֹא תִירָאוּ` → *Fear ye not me*. Two limits. Where no interrogative morpheme is present at all, a fronted *do* is the verb's own under this rule's first sentence: `לֹא שָׁפָטוּ` → *do they not judge*. And this governs the yes-or-no particle only: an interrogative word that has an English word of its own — `מָה` → *what*, `אֵי` → *How* — leaves the fronted auxiliary to the verb, as `אֵי לָזֹאת אֶסְלַח לָךְ` → *How can I pardon thee* leaves *can I pardon* whole. **And a particle heading an indirect question takes the subordinating word the ASV writes for it, which puts it in that same position.** Where `הֲ` introduces a question embedded under a verb of testing, seeing, knowing or asking and the ASV writes *whether* or *if* at the head of the embedded clause, that word is what the particle is rendered by: the particle takes it and heads on it, and a modal or auxiliary the ASV fronts inside that clause belongs to the predicate under this rule's first sentence. `לְמַעַן נַסּוֹת בָּם אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל הֲשֹׁמְרִים הֵם אֶת־דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה` → *that I may prove Israel,* ***whether*** *they* ***will keep*** *the way of Jehovah* gives *whether* to `הֲ` and *will keep* to the participial predicate, while the explicit pronoun keeps only its own *they* under rule 20. This is the count the paragraph above runs, read for the first question rather than the second: a particle already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and giving it both would leave the predicate's auxiliary unaccounted against rule 2. The corpus aligns an interrogative `הַ` to *whether* in six units. Read what the ASV has written before reaching for this sentence: where it marks the embedded question by the fronted auxiliary alone and writes no subordinator, the particle takes that auxiliary as in a direct question, and where it writes neither, the particle is `unrepresented` as above. **An English matrix duration frame is not an auxiliary of the finite verb inside the temporal clause it introduces.** Where `עַד` plus a temporal interrogative and `לֹא` plus a finite verb is rendered *how long will it be ere ...*, the temporal-interrogative expression takes *how long will it be* as one `noncompositional` unit, headed on *long*; the negative takes *ere*; and the finite verb takes only its subordinate subject and predicate. `עַד מָתַי לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *how long will it be ere they attain* and `עַד אָנָה לֹא תִשְׁקֹטִי` → *how long will it be ere thou be quiet* follow that division. The dummy *it* is not the finite verb's person and number, and assigning the matrix frame to that verb would give it two English clauses. This does not make a simple *how long ...* indivisible where the ASV writes no separate matrix frame; there each morpheme is aligned on its own merits under rule 2. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus a finite verb as a relative clause and no explicit subject pronoun in that clause is realized by that relative, the relative *who* or *which* is the connective the ASV has written for the waw and belongs to the waw; the verb keeps its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb.** `וַתֹּאכַל` → *which hath devoured* gives *which* to the waw and *hath devoured* to the verb. This is the other side of the explicit-pronoun case above: a pronoun the relative realizes takes it before the waw does, but a pronoun standing in the clause under an English word of its own is not such a pronoun, and without one the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective. Where no waw or other conjunction stands either, rule 55 governs the supplied relative instead. The finished corpus aligns a waw directly to *which* in ten units, so this is settled rather than a tie to hedge.
amendments.why: 1SA.10.24 marked the italic *Long* of *Long live the king* `added`, while the corpus reads the same jussive acclamation as one *Long live* unit headed on *live* in 1KI.1.25, 1KI.1.34, 1KI.1.39 and 2CH.23.11 (two of those notes name the `added` reading as the competing one, so passes keep hesitating). Rule 17's volitive-frame sentence already covers it in principle but named only the *Oh* frames; adding the acclamation as a named example closes the gap without changing any other clause. The rule's two trailing paragraphs that duplicated its own matrix-duration and waw-relative sentences are not repeated here, since the refined versions stand inside the rule.

conventions: A waw whose own clause the ASV recasts as a subordinate one, writing *And when*, *and when* or *but when* contiguously at that clause's left edge (10.10, 10.13, 10.14, 10.21, 10.23), takes both words as one unit under rule 55 and is headed on the coordinator throughout this chapter; the corpus heads a minority of such units on *when*, which is the competing reading. A bare *when* the ASV separates from the *And* (10.11, where *And* belongs to the וַיְהִי waw) goes to the protasis waw alone.

`שָׁאַל לְ + suffix לְשָׁלוֹם` → *salute thee* (10.4): the one English verb goes to `שָׁאַל`, both `לְ`s are `unrepresented` under rule 40, and `שָׁלוֹם` is its own `unrepresented` unit. Rule 30 fusion is barred because the object `לְךָ` stands between the verb and `לְשָׁלוֹם`, and the corpus has no precedent for this idiom either way.

`צָלַח` → *come mightily* / *came mightily* (10.6, 10.10) is one unit headed on the verb, as in JDG.14.6, JDG.14.19 and JDG.15.14; heading on *mightily* under rule 44's light-verb test is the competing reading. `מֵעִם` → *from* (10.2, 10.9) fuses under rule 30 and heads on the governing `מִן` under rule 23, as `מֵאֵת` does.

And this governs the yes-or-no particle only: an interrogative word that has an English word of its own — `מָה` → *what*, `אֵי` → *How* — leaves the fronted auxiliary to the verb, as `אֵי לָזֹאת אֶסְלַח לָךְ` → *How can I pardon thee* leaves *can I pardon* whole. **And a particle heading an indirect question takes the subordinating word the ASV writes for it, which puts it in that same position.** Where `הֲ` introduces a question embedded under a verb of testing, seeing, knowing or asking and the ASV writes *whether* or *if* at the head of the embedded clause, that word is what the particle is rendered by: the particle takes it and heads on it, and a modal or auxiliary the ASV fronts inside that clause belongs to the predicate under this rule's first sentence. `לְמַעַן נַסּוֹת בָּם אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל הֲשֹׁמְרִים הֵם אֶת־דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה` → *that I may prove Israel,* ***whether*** *they* ***will keep*** *the way of Jehovah* gives *whether* to `הֲ` and *will keep* to the participial predicate, while the explicit pronoun keeps only its own *they* under rule 20. This is the count the paragraph above runs, read for the first question rather than the second: a particle already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and giving it both would leave the predicate's auxiliary unaccounted against rule 2. The corpus aligns an interrogative `הַ` to *whether* in six units. Read what the ASV has written before reaching for this sentence: where it marks the embedded question by the fronted auxiliary alone and writes no subordinator, the particle takes that auxiliary as in a direct question, and where it writes neither, the particle is `unrepresented` as above. **An English matrix duration frame is not an auxiliary of the finite verb inside the temporal clause it introduces.** Where `עַד` plus a temporal interrogative and `לֹא` plus a finite verb is rendered *how long will it be ere ...*, the temporal-interrogative expression takes *how long will it be* as one `noncompositional` unit, headed on *long*; the negative takes *ere*; and the finite verb takes only its subordinate subject and predicate. `עַד מָתַי לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *how long will it be ere they attain* and `עַד אָנָה לֹא תִשְׁקֹטִי` → *how long will it be ere thou be quiet* follow that division. The dummy *it* is not the finite verb's person and number, and assigning the matrix frame to that verb would give it two English clauses. This does not make a simple *how long ...* indivisible where the ASV writes no separate matrix frame; there each morpheme is aligned on its own merits under rule 2. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus a finite verb as a relative clause and no explicit subject pronoun in that clause is realized by that relative, the relative *who* or *which* is the connective the ASV has written for the waw and belongs to the waw; the verb keeps its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb.** `וַתֹּאכַל` → *which hath devoured* gives *which* to the waw and *hath devoured* to the verb. This is the other side of the explicit-pronoun case above: a pronoun the relative realizes takes it before the waw does, but a pronoun standing in the clause under an English word of its own is not such a pronoun, and without one the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective. Where no waw or other conjunction stands either, rule 55 governs the supplied relative instead. The finished corpus aligns a waw directly to *which* in ten units, so this is settled rather than a tie to hedge.
amended.why: 1SA.10.24 marked the italic *Long* of *Long live the king* `added`, while the corpus reads the same jussive acclamation as one *Long live* unit headed on *live* in 1KI.1.25, 1KI.1.34, 1KI.1.39 and 2CH.23.11 (two of those notes name the `added` reading as the competing one, so passes keep hesitating). Rule 17's volitive-frame sentence already covers it in principle but named only the *Oh* frames; adding the acclamation as a named example closes the gap without changing any other clause. The rule's two trailing paragraphs that duplicated its own matrix-duration and waw-relative sentences are not repeated here, since the refined versions stand inside the rule.

report: Read all 68 candidate groups end to end. Every waw, article, לְ, אֵת, אֶל, בְּ, מִן, כֹּל, שָׁם and suffix difference is licensed by a different ASV rendering (e.g. מִשָּׁם → *from thence* split in 10.3 but fused to a bare *thence* in 10.23; הָאֱלֹהִים → *the hill of God* fronted in 10.5 but *God* bare in 10.3/10.7; לְמָשָׁל left unrepresented beside a written הָיָה in 10.12 under rule 21 while לְנָגִיד takes *to be* in 10.1 under rule 49). No cross-verse split found among those.

One correction, from the evidence round: 1SA.10.24 marked the italic *Long* of *Long live the king* `added`. The corpus reads the jussive acclamation יְחִי → *Long live* in every unit it records (1KI.1.25, 1KI.1.34, 1KI.1.39, 2CH.23.11), all headed on *live*, and 2CH.23.11's note reasons it under rule 17's volitive-frame sentence. Patched 10.24 to give *Long live* to יְחִי, headed on *live*; the italic corroborates the supply and decides nothing (rule 7). Amended rule 17 to name the acclamation so a later verse pass does not re-derive it.
צָלַח → *come mightily* / *came mightily* (10.6, 10.10) heads on the verb, agreeing with all three JDG corpus units; no change.

שָׁלוֹם in שָׁאֲלוּ לְךָ לְשָׁלוֹם → *salute thee* (10.4) is unrepresented; the corpus has no precedent either way. The reading follows rule 30's contiguity clause (the object לְךָ stands between the verb and לְשָׁלוֹם, so the idiom cannot fuse) and stands; recorded as a convention since the idiom recurs in Samuel.

BSB disagreements: all convention. The R/C/Td classes are the documented differences; דִּבְרֵי (10.2) and שָׁלוֹם (10.4) are nouns the ASV's recasting leaves without a word; the 10.7 לְךָ suffix is an ethical dative the ASV drops (its *thee* answers to the יָדֶךָ suffix); 10.9 בַּ is a bare *that day*; 10.11 רֵעֵהוּ is *another* with no possessive; 10.24 בּוֹ is the resumptive suffix rule 22 leaves unrepresented; 10.15 Sh, 10.18 אֶתְכֶם and 10.24 הַ (question recast as the imperative *See ye*) have nothing written for them. None is an error.

The five *And when*/*and when*/*but when* waws (10.10, 10.13, 10.14, 10.21, 10.23) were corrected by the verse passes to one unit each under rule 55 and all head on the coordinator; recorded as a convention because the corpus heads a minority of such units on *when*.
